extracted.intended_audience: Press Gazette readers — journalists, editors, PRs and other UK media professionals
extracted.subtask_description: An event announcement and commentary inviting Press Gazette readers to a public debate on Nick Davies' book Flat Earth News and the issue of 'churnalism' in UK journalism. Includes panel listing, event logistics and ticket application instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is a culture of 'churnalism' destroying real journalism?
rubrics_metrics.description: Framed as the central question of Nick Davies' book Flat Earth News and the debate: whether recycled PR and news-agency copy have replaced original journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davies uses academic research to argue that the majority of news content in the UK national press is made up of recycled PR and news agency copy. Evaluate stories for their originality and the degree to which they derive from PR/agency material rather than original reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on recycled PR and news agency copy
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which news content is composed of reused PR or agency material rather than independently sourced reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for provenance of copy — is the story adapted from PR material or agency dispatches? Anti-pattern: stories that mirror press releases verbatim or that reproduce agency copy without additional reporting or verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism and verification of PRs, vested interests and governments
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether journalists critically assess and independently verify claims coming from public relations sources, vested interests and government statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davies alleges journalists have been 'hoodwinked' on stories (examples cited: millennium bug, WMD, Iraq). Good practice is independent fact-checking and not accepting claims at face value; poor practice is uncritical repetition of source claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-the-ground reporting and meeting real people
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists spending time meeting sources and reporting from the field rather than producing desk-based copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davies criticises regional press practices where journalists are 'chained to their desks churning out stories and hardly ever meeting real people face to face.' Quality journalism involves direct engagement with sources, original interviews and first‑hand reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work practices and newsroom pressures affecting quality
rubrics_metrics.description: How newsroom working conditions (e.g., heavy workloads, desk-bound routines) influence the quality and authenticity of journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether structural factors — staffing, time pressures, production targets — lead to churned output. Consider whether editorial workflows encourage verification and original reporting or prioritize volume over depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical scrutiny of individual news organisations' journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissecting the editorial and sourcing practices of specific news organisations to assess their contribution to churnalism or original reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davies 'dissects the journalism of specific news organisations' — evaluators should examine case studies of coverage, trace sourcing, and judge institutional practices rather than treating the press as monolithic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition for balanced debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Including a range of stakeholders (investigative journalists, editors, union representatives, PR executives) when debating journalism standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press Gazette assembled a panel including Nick Davies (Guardian), Andrew Gilligan (investigative reporter), Malcom Starbrook (editor/PCC member), Michelle Stanistreet (NUJ president), Sally Costerton (PR firm chief) — exemplifying a cross‑sector group to cover multiple perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event/ticket application requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions and required information for securing free tickets to the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To apply for one of 100 free tickets readers must email Alexandra Pont with their name, job title and company. Organisers expect high demand and advise prompt responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event logistics and audience participation expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical details that set expectations for attendees and the format of the debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The debate takes place 7pm–9pm at the London College of Communications, with free drinks and refreshments before and after, and 'ample opportunity to ask questions and debate the issues on the floor' — indicating a public Q&A format.
